Chapter 1: Rethinking Faith as a Living, Changing Journey
You know, there’s just something comforting about things that never change. Maybe it’s that old family photo hanging on the wall, the one that’s always been there. Or the familiar creak of a floorboard in your childhood home.
For a lot of people, faith has felt just like that—solid, unmoving, a set of beliefs passed down and carefully protected.
But life doesn’t stay still, does it? And sometimes, the way we look at faith starts to shift, too. Questions can sneak up on us—maybe during a quiet moment in church, or while reading a story that just doesn’t seem to fit anymore. Suddenly, the old answers don’t always work, and that gentle urge to ask, to wonder, grows stronger.
Picture this: you’re standing right in the middle of that tension. Maybe you’re a young adult who grew up memorizing Bible verses. Or maybe you’re a parent, watching your kids drift away from church. You remember being told that faith is supposed to be like a brick wall—each belief stacked on another, building a strong structure to keep everything safe.
But what if one brick just doesn’t fit? Or a single question shakes the whole wall? It’s a real fear—if one part crumbles, does everything else come crashing down?
And yet, in moments like these, something new can begin to take shape. Instead of seeing faith as a wall, what if it’s more like a trampoline? Something flexible, something that moves and stretches. Not just there for protection, but to invite play and exploration. The springs of the trampoline are like our beliefs and teachings, but the point isn’t to defend every single spring—it’s to feel the joy of bouncing, of living, of asking and discovering.
Of course, making this shift isn’t easy. There’s this story about someone who spent years teaching Sunday school. One day, a child asked a question about a Bible story, and suddenly, all the old explanations felt a little thin. It would’ve been easy to just pretend or gloss over the uncertainty. But instead, they admitted, “I don’t know.” The room got quiet. Then, something amazing happened—the kids leaned in, curious, and the conversation opened up. Not knowing wasn’t a failure. It was an invitation—to wonder, to search, to grow together.
Most of us don’t notice how much our faith is shaped by the world around us. The language we use, the customs we follow, even the way stories are told—they’re all filtered through culture and time. What made sense centuries ago might not answer today’s questions. But still, there’s this urge to cling to the past, to treat every tradition as untouchable, even when it doesn’t bring life anymore.
At the heart of this new approach is humility. It means admitting that no one has all the answers, and that faith isn’t about having everything figured out. It’s about being open to change, to learning, and to repainting what it really means to follow Jesus. This doesn’t mean tossing out everything that came before—it just means holding onto our beliefs with open hands. We let go of what no longer fits, and make room for what brings deeper understanding.
In the end, faith becomes something alive—something that grows and adapts, that makes space for questions and doubts along the way. The old fear of losing everything starts to fade, replaced by the excitement of discovery. Because the story of faith isn’t finished. It’s being written every single day, in every life that’s willing to ask, to seek, and to believe there’s always more to learn.
